new_statements.quote: [2.1.2, p. 21] The DD tone system is close to that of Donno So (Kamma So), i.e. a semi-pitch accent system with exactly one lexical H-tone per stem, realized on a single syllable or (in the case of a rising tone) on the final mora of a heavy syllable. [3.7, p. 39] At least in the speech of my primary informant (from Koundiala village), DD has a tone system resembling pitch accent. [3.7.1.1, p. 40] In this type of system, each stem has one lexical H-tone, expressed on one entire syllable or on one syllable-final mora. Bisyllabics therefore are either Cv́Cv̀ or Cv̀Cv́, but not #Cv́Cv́ and not (lexically) Cv̀Cv̀ [...] [3.7.1.6, p. 42] DD allows only one accented syllable
new_statements.citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2016. A Grammar of Dogul Dom (Dogon language family, Mali). Draft of July 2016, University of Michigan; Language Description Heritage Library (MPG PuRe item_2326691).
new_statements.locator: Sec. 2.1.2 Prosody, p. 21 (PDF p. 22); sec. 3.7 Tones, p. 39 (PDF p. 40); sec. 3.7.1.1, p. 40 (PDF p. 41); sec. 3.7.1.6, p. 42 (PDF p. 43)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dogul Dom is described as a tone language of the (semi-)pitch-accent type: every stem carries exactly one lexical H tone ('one accented syllable'), whose position is lexically specified (/HL/ vs /LH/ melodies: H on the first syllable, or on the final syllable/final mora); no word stress independent of tone is described. The only metrical remark is that the medial syllable of CvCvCv verb stems is weak (vowel raising, syncope).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. The one-H-per-stem rule does not hold at word level: suffixed verbs may carry two separate H-tones (e.g. imperfective negative bɔ́lɛ̀-nnú-), p. 40.
new_statements.exceptions: Stems can surface all-L through tonosyntactic {L} overlays or Rightward H-Tone Shift (LH#LL -> LL#HL); final long vowels of nonmonosyllabic stems conflate H and <HL>; characterization explicitly hedged to the primary informant's (Koundiala) speech and attributed possibly to contact with Donno So.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of the one-H constraint is the stem (lexical melody), not the inflected word; grammatical tone overlays operate over words and multi-word NP strings.
new_statements.identity_note: Heath 2016 describes Dogul Dom (dogu1235, ISO dbg) as a whole; elicited data almost entirely from one speaker from Koundiala village (western/central DD area), texts from Nantanga (eastern area). Heath explicitly restricts the pitch-accent characterization to 'at least the speech of my primary informant (from Koundiala village)'. No sub-dialect glottocodes exist.

sources.note: No stress section. Prosody is described as tonal, 'a semi-pitch accent system with exactly one lexical H-tone per stem' (2.1.2, p. 21); 'DD has a tone system resembling pitch accent' (3.7, p. 39); 'DD allows only one accented syllable' (3.7.1.6, p. 42); position of the H is lexical (/HL/ vs /LH/ melodies; bisyllabics Cv́Cv̀ or Cv̀Cv́, 3.7.1.1 p. 40). 3.2.2 (p. 25): medial syllable of CvCvCv verb stems is metrically weak (raising/syncope). The word 'stressed' appears only for rhetorical lengthening of fà→ (3.8.1, p. 53).
